years, what did you find?
Karen Canfell: So we found that there has been this great reduction of 50% or
more in women over the age of 25, and in fact that reduction holds over beyond
the age of stopping screening. So we found this similar reduction even in women
over the age of 70 who aren't targeted by the screening program. So that's
fantastic. It shows that there is long-term hold-over benefits from regular
screening. We found that there were no changes in rates in younger women
under the age of 25.
Norman Swan: So screening made no difference to them?
Karen Canfell: Screening made no difference over the 20-year period.
Norman Swan: Well, the good news in that is that starting at 25 is not going to
make any difference in theory. But why is it not making any impact?
Karen Canfell: Well, the new program, first of all to say it's predicted to be 20%
even more effective than the current program, so there's that…
Norman Swan: Okay, that's the PR, but let's go to…I'm being cynical, but just tell
me why under the 25 it had no impact. Is that a different kind of cancer or…?
Karen Canfell: Well, there's a few reasons and it is consistent with a lot of
international evidence. First of all, cervical cancer is very, very rare in that age
group. Secondly, we have a lot of evidence that the testing doesn't pick it up well.
It may be that there is a rare subtype of cancer that is more aggressive, but we
have a lot of data now that shows that screening makes no impact in that age
group, and I think the new study today just confirms that in the Australian context.
